lead: Welding joins metal parts by melting metal at the joint. A weld is sized by the area that carries load: the throat. Once throat area and the second moment of the weld lines about the group centroid are known, an eccentric load splits into a direct part and a moment part, as in a bolted joint. Brackets, frames, trusses and nozzles are sized this way.
prereq: You need Unit 1 for direct, bending and torsion stress, and chapter 4.1 for the direct-plus-moment split of an eccentric load.

sections.h3: Butt welds, fillet welds and the throat

blocks.text: Two shapes carry most loads. A butt weld joins plates edge to edge and fills the thickness; load crosses the weld, so throat equals plate thickness t. A fillet weld joins surfaces at a corner and has triangular section. Its weakest plane is the throat at 45°: t = 0.707h, where h is leg size, the dimension beside the weld symbol.

The 0.707 is geometry. An equal-leg fillet has legs h and h, so throat is h·cos 45° = 0.707h. Stress is uniform over throat. Use effective length L = actual length − 2h, allowing for start and stop craters.

blocks.where: τ is shear stress on the throat in N/mm² (MPa); P is the axial load in N; h is the leg size in mm; L is the effective length in mm. For a butt weld, replace 0.707h by the plate thickness t.

blocks.text: Drawing carries h and L through the symbol: triangle on reference line means fillet, size left, length right. Read symbol first. Leg size, not plate thickness, enters the formula.

sections.h3: Eccentric load in the plane of the welds

blocks.text: An eccentric load does not pass through the weld-group centroid. Replace it by the same P at centroid plus torque T = P·e, where e is perpendicular distance in mm from centroid to line of action.

Direct part: τ_d = P/A_w with A_w = t·ΣL. It has direction of P and same value everywhere. Torque part: τ_t = T·r/J_w; r is distance in mm from centroid to point; J_w is polar second moment of throat area about centroid. It acts perpendicular to r.

J_w for a thin shape by the weld-line method: weld as zero-thickness lines. A_w = t·A_line and J_w = t·J_line, where A_line = ΣL in mm, J_line = Σ(L³/12 + L·d²) in mm³, and d is perpendicular distance from the weld line to the parallel axis through the group centroid. A throat thickness t multiplies every area element, so it multiplies both quantities.

items: Mark the weld group and find the centroid. For two equal parallel welds it lies midway between them.
Compute A_line = ΣL in mm and J_line = Σ(L³/12 + L·d²) in mm³.
Direct shear τ_d = P/(t·A_line), same everywhere, along P.
Torsional shear τ_t = T·r/(t·J_line) at the trial point, perpendicular to r.
Add the two as vectors at each trial point; keep the largest resultant.

blocks.text: τ_max = √(τ_d² + τ_t² + 2 τ_d τ_t cos θ)
blocks.where: τ_d is the direct shear in MPa; τ_t is the torsional shear at that point in MPa; θ is the angle between their directions at that point. Plain addition of the two numbers is wrong.

sections.h3: Out-of-plane load and the allowable stress

blocks.text: When the load is perpendicular to the plane of the weld group it produces bending about an axis through the centroid, not torsion. M = P·e bends the group; stress at distance y from the neutral axis is M·y/I_w, with I_w = t·I_line and I_line about that axis. Add direct stress P/A_w algebraically, since both act on the same throat plane in the same sense.

For a fillet weld both stresses are taken on the throat; they act in the same direction, so add them algebraically: τ_total = P/A_w + M·y/I_w. Vector addition is needed only for the in-plane case of Section 2. For a butt weld bending stress is normal to the throat, so it adds directly to the axial stress and the total is compared with the permissible tensile value.

Permissible stress comes from yield and factor of safety. Distortion-energy theory gives shear yield σ_y/√3 ≈ 0.577σ_y, so τ_perm = 0.577σ_y/FOS. Codes publish lower values for weld metal, electrodes and service conditions; use code value when a code applies. Weld fatigue is separate (Unit 2).

figure.caption: One eccentric load becomes a throat area and a line polar moment, then a direct shear and a torsional shear that must be added as vectors. Torsion dominates here: torsional shear is about three times direct shear.

spec.title: Eccentric fillet weld
spec.aria: The weld group gives a throat area and a polar moment, which turn the load and the torque into a direct shear and a torsional shear that meet at the critical weld point.

examples.question: Two vertical parallel fillet welds, each with effective length L = 100 mm and leg h = 6 mm, are 100 mm apart centre to centre. A vertical load P = 10 kN acts in the plane of the welds at e = 150 mm from the centroid of the group. Find the maximum resultant shear stress on the throat.
steps: Throat area A_w = 2 × t × L = 2 × 4.24 × 100 = 848.4 mm².
Direct shear τ_d = P/A_w = 10 000/848.4 = 11.8 MPa, vertical, same at every point.
Trial points: the two ends of the weld nearer the line of action, r = √(50² + 50²) = 70.7 mm.
Torsional shear τ_t = T·r/J_w = 1.5 × 10⁶ × 70.7 / 2.83 × 10⁶ = 37.5 MPa, perpendicular to r, that is at 45° to the vertical.
At a near-weld end, vertical component = 11.8 + 37.5 × 0.707 = 38.3 MPa. Horizontal component = 37.5 × 0.707 = 26.5 MPa.
examples.answer: Maximum resultant shear stress is 46.6 MPa at the two ends of the weld nearer the line of action. The ends of the far weld give about 30.3 MPa. Compare with τ_perm = 0.577σ_y/FOS.
examples.check:
import math
P = 10000.0
e = 150.0
L = 100.0
h = 6.0
d = 100.0
t = 0.707*h
A = 2*t*L
td = P/A
T = P*e
Jline = 2*(L**3/12 + L*(d/2)**2)
J = t*Jline
r = math.hypot(d/2, L/2)
tt = T*r/J
vy = td + tt*(d/2)/r
vx = tt*(L/2)/r
res = math.hypot(vx, vy)
print(round(A,1))
print(round(td,1))
print(round(J/1e6,2))
print(round(r,1))
print(round(tt,1))
print(round(res,1))

traps: Using leg size h as the throat. For a fillet weld the throat is 0.707h, so the wrong choice gives τ = P/(hL) = 0.707 × true stress: stress is understated by about 29%; true stress is about 41% higher than the wrong answer.
Adding direct and torsional shear as plain numbers. They act at an angle and must be added as vectors.
Using J of a solid rectangle instead of the weld line, or using the line value without multiplying by the throat thickness.
Assuming the farthest point is always critical. At a nearer point the two shears can line up and give a larger resultant.
Mixing units: torque in kN·m with r in mm. Work throughout in N and mm.

quiz.q: Why is the throat of an equal-leg fillet weld 0.707h?
quiz.a: The throat is the shortest distance from the corner to the hypotenuse of the triangular section; for legs h and h it is h·cos 45° = 0.707h.
Treating the weld as zero-thickness lines to get A_line and J_line, then multiplying both by the throat thickness t to get the real throat area and polar moment.

quiz.q: Why is the direct shear the same at every point of the weld group while the torsional shear is not?
quiz.a: The direct load is shared by the whole throat area equally. The torque produces a shear proportional to r, so points farther from the centroid carry more.

quiz.q: A single fillet weld of leg 8 mm and effective length 150 mm carries an axial load of 30 kN. Find the shear stress on the throat.

Two parallel fillet welds, each with effective length L = 80 mm and leg 5 mm, are 60 mm apart. A load of 6 kN acts in the plane, parallel to the welds, at 100 mm from the centroid. Find the maximum throat shear.
For a single long weld, why does torsional shear fall faster than direct shear as L increases?
quiz.a: Area grows as L, so direct shear falls as 1/L. For one long weld J_line ≈ L³/12 grows as L³ and r also grows with L, so torsional shear falls as about 1/L². For two well-separated welds J_line grows mostly as L·d², so both fall at similar rates.

quiz.q: An out-of-plane load acts on a bracket with two fillet welds. Why can the bending stress and the direct stress be added algebraically here, while an in-plane load needs a vector sum?
quiz.a: Out of plane, both stresses act on the same throat plane in the same sense, so they add as numbers. In plane, the direct shear and the torsional shear point in different directions and must be combined as vectors.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real welds carry residual stress, undercut and slag inclusions that act as stress raisers, and codes such as AWS D1.1 or ISO 2553 fix both symbol grammar and allowable values. Finite element models resolve the throat stress gradient that the weld-line method averages away. Welding robots and laser-hybrid processes change the heat-affected zone, so weldability of the base metal matters as much as the arithmetic. Useful search terms: weld throat effective length, weld group polar moment, AWS D1.1 allowable shear, heat-affected zone softening.
